title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
hook: Radio, microwaves, the warmth of sunlight, the colors you see, and a hospital X-ray are all the same thing — electromagnetic waves, differing only in wavelength.
key_points: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma are one family of electromagnetic waves.
They differ only in wavelength and frequency, not in their underlying nature.
Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and higher energy per photon.
Visible light is a tiny slice of the full spectrum, the part our eyes evolved to see.
content_html: It's tempting to think radio waves, the heat from a fire, the colors of a sunset, and a medical X-ray are unrelated. They're not. Every one of them is an electromagnetic wave, and the only thing that changes from one to the next is the wavelength — how far apart the wave's peaks are — and the matching frequency.
extra_html: Line them up from longest wavelength to shortest and you get the electromagnetic spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency, which means more energy per photon — that's why gamma rays are dangerous and radio waves pass through you harmlessly. The colors your eyes can see make up just a sliver in the middle, the band where the Sun shines brightest and our vision evolved to take advantage of it. Wikipedia lays out the full lineup band by band.

related.title: Is Light a Wave or a Particle?
related.hook: Light behaves like a wave in some experiments and like a stream of particles in others — and the surprising answer is that it's both.

related.title: Electricity & Magnetism Are One Force
related.hook: Move a magnet near a wire and you make electricity; run current through a wire and you make a magnet. They're two faces of the same force.

related.title: A Material That Turns Sunlight Into UV Light
related.hook: A new solid material soaks up ordinary visible sunlight and re-emits it as higher-energy ultraviolet — running uphill in energy, which light rarely does on its own.

flashcards.prompt: What do radio waves, visible light, and X-rays have in common?
flashcards.back_html: They are all electromagnetic waves — the same kind of wave, differing only in wavelength and frequency.

flashcards.prompt: Across the electromagnetic spectrum, shorter wavelength means...
flashcards.explanation_html: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related, and higher-frequency waves carry more energy per photon — so gamma rays pack far more punch than radio.

flashcards.prompt: Where does visible light sit in the spectrum?

choices.text: It's a tiny slice in the middle, the part our eyes can detect
It covers most of the spectrum
It's a separate phenomenon, not electromagnetic

flashcards.explanation_html: Visible light spans only a narrow band of wavelengths; the spectrum extends far beyond it in both directions, from radio to gamma rays.
